articles.title: Ranking Padres SP Michael King, Casey Mize's Top Landing Spots Ahead of MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: Though the wounds of San Diego's NLDS exit from the postseason are still painfully fresh, the Padres need to quickly turn their focus to what will be a particularly eventful offseason for them.
articles.body:
Though the wounds of San Diego's NLDS exit from the postseason are still painfully fresh, the Padres need to quickly turn their focus to what will be a particularly eventful offseason for them.

They have nine unrestricted free agents, three players with mutual options (who might as well be unrestricted free agents), plus three more with player options. That could mean as many as 15 holes to fill, and in a winter that could also be complicated by a lockout.

Two of their biggest soon-to-be free agents are starting pitchers Michael King and Casey Mize. The latter is one of the nine unrestricted FAs, while the former is very likely to exercise an opt-out clause to hit the open market for a second consecutive year.

Will either (or both?) of those righties re-sign with the Padres, or where do they best fit for 2027 and beyond?

Ahead, we've put together a ranking of what we believe to be the best landing spots for each, starting with Mize before diving deeper into the teams most likely to pay...a King's ransom.

Though Michael King and Casey Mize are both right-handed starting pitchers with an injury history who ended the year with the San Diego Padres, the similarities arguably end there.

King has been, when healthy, one of the better pitchers of the past half-decade.

If that feels like hyperbole, please note that he is one of just eight pitchers with at least 450 innings pitched and an ERA of 3.00 or better since the beginning of 2022. The others on that list are Paul Skenes, Tarik Skubal, Blake Snell, Chris Sale, Max Fried, Zack Wheeler and the patron saint of "really good when healthy" Drew Rasmussen.

King also has a 1.86 ERA in seven career postseason appearances, including that gutsy two-inning save in Game 3 against Milwaukee.

Despite missing half of last season, he signed a three-year, $75M contract this past December, with player options after each of the first two seasons. It is a near certainty that he will opt out, though, after he spent the past six months almost single-handedly carrying San Diego's starting rotation, never missing a start.

He turns 32 in May, so he probably won't quite fetch a Fried-sized contract—eight years, $218M; signed one month before his 31st birthday and two days after the Yankees lost Juan Soto to the Mets. But King should have no problem whatsoever fetching nine figures on a five-year deal.

And then there's Mize, who was taken No. 1 overall in the 2018 draft and has had flashes/stretches of brilliance, but simply has not lived up to the hype that comes with that distinction.

Mize had a 2.70 ERA in 16 starts with the Tigers this season, but gave the Padres a disastrous 7.46 ERA after the trade deadline before landing on the IL for the third time this season—a near-perfect encapsulation of a career in which he has yet to log enough innings for an ERA title and seems to have a six-week-long rough patch in each season.

In other words, he's a wild card, much like Tyler Mahle has been both previous times he hit free agency, ending up with short-term contracts with an AAV of around $10M.

Had Mize's brief time with San Diego gone better, he probably could have commanded much more than that on the open market. As is, $10M for one year or $20M for two years feels about right, which means just about any team could acquire him.

Casey Mize Landing Spot No. 3: Detroit Tigers

Projected 2027 Starting Rotation Options : Framber Valdez, Troy Melton, Keider Montero, Jackson Jobe, Drew Anderson, River Ryan?, Reese Olson??

Even though the San Diego Padres head into the offseason in desperate need of starting pitching, it's hard to imagine they'll have any interest in re-upping with Mize. He had an 8.28 ERA and no quality starts over his final seven appearances. At this point, they're just hoping they don't also live to regret parting with 2024 first-round pick Kash Mayfield to acquire Mize.

A different reunion could be in the cards for Mize, though, as Detroit also clearly needs starting pitching, moving on without what had been the Nos. 1, 3, 4 and 5 starters in its Opening Day rotation.

What we don't know is whether Mize would have any interest in returning to Motown after they never even approached him about a contract extension before trading him away, per Bob Nightengale . If there's lingering animosity about the way things ended, go ahead and scratch Detroit from the list of candidates.

Sometimes, though, you just want to go where everybody knows your name. And Mize did have a solid run over the past two seasons at Comerica Park, making 22 starts with a 3.18 ERA.

Casey Mize Landing Spot No. 2: Atlanta Braves

Projected 2027 Starting Rotation Options : Chris Sale, Spencer Strider, Grant Holmes, Bryce Elder, JR Ritchie, AJ Smith-Shawver, Spencer Schwellenbach

Mize is from Springville, Alabama. He went to college at Auburn. He presently lives in Nashville.

For all three of those locations, the nearest MLB stadium is Truist Park in Atlanta.

Mize grew up as a big fan of Derek Jeter and the Yankees, so pitching for the Braves wouldn't exactly fulfill a lifelong dream of his. (Before you ask, the Yankees do not figure to be adding any starting pitchers this winter.) However, getting to make home starts within a reasonable drive of his various homes could be a nice selling point in free agency.

And the Braves sure could use another pitcher for their deep stable of once-promising arms that can never seem to stay healthy.

While Schwellenbach missed all of 2026 and Strider and Smith-Shawver both made just eight appearances, Elder (4.62), Holmes (4.76) and Ritchie (5.54) each posted FIPs that left much to be desired.

Sale had a Cy Young-caliber year, but he turns 38 in March and was already getting at least five days' rest after nearly every start this season.

The Braves do already have 12 players signed for a combined sum of $190M in 2027, though, and also have to figure out what to do about the impending departures of Raisel Iglesias and Mauricio Dubón. That likely means targeting someone like Mize as opposed to making a serious push for a Tarik Skubal or Michael King type of contract.

Predicting the Outcome for Each Team's Top Free Agent 🔮

Casey Mize Landing Spot No. 1: San Francisco Giants

Projected 2027 Starting Rotation Options : Logan Webb, Landen Roupp, Adrian Houser, Matt Wilkinson, Anthony Molina

Eight pitchers made at least eight starts for the Giants in 2026.

From that bunch, Robbie Ray and Tyler Mahle were traded away in August, and Trevor McDonald, Carson Whisenhunt and Blade Tidwell are most likely going to miss all of 2027 following recent Tommy John surgeries.

Adrian Houser also missed the final month of the regular season with an elbow injury and had already lost his starting job anyway, posting a 5.73 ERA in his first 14 appearances.

So, San Francisco's rotation outlook is Logan Webb, Landen Roupp and a bay full of question marks.

With how much money the Giants have tied up in Rafael Devers, Matt Chapman, Willy Adames, Jung Hoo Lee, Webb and Houser, though, they kind of have to at least try to cobble together a competent rotation.

And Mize would fit right into their free agency wheelhouse: Spending $10M-$15M per year on short-term deals with guys who might be No. 3 starters in an ideal world.

They did make that one late-in-the-offseason splash for Blake Snell before the 2024 campaign, and took a similar "one year plus a player option" gamble on the oft-injured Carlos Rodón prior to 2022. But every other free agent starting pitcher they've signed in the past half-decade—Alex Cobb, Alex Wood, Anthony DeSclafani, Sean Manaea, Ross Stripling, Jordan Hicks, Justin Verlander, Mahle and Houser—has fit that "12-ish million per year for a maybe middle-of-the-rotation guy" description.

Granted, it hasn't been working for them, last posting a winning record in 2021. It might be time to abandon that approach to roster building. But Mize is exactly the type of player they usually target.

Honorable Mentions for Michael King Landing Spots

Arizona Diamondbacks : Over the past three offseasons, Arizona has signed five starting pitchers to contracts with an AAV of at least $20M. They do still have Corbin Burnes, Merrill Kelly and Eduardo Rodriguez on the payroll, but they might be a little extra desperate this winter after landing on the wrong end of yet another photo finish on the final day of the regular season.

Chicago White Sox : 2026 was the surprise breakthrough, but now is the time to double down on this newfound window of relevance. For now, the White Sox have five known salary figures for 2027, totaling less than $70M. Add in their four arbitration-eligible players and we're maybe talking $85M—for a club that had a payroll north of $200M in 2022 and 2023. They're going to do something big, and it ought to be in the starting rotation.

Houston Astros : Unless they trade away one of Christian Walker, Isaac Paredes or Jeremy Peña and/or unless Tatsuya Imai makes the surprising decision to decline his $18M player option, Houston probably doesn't have room in the 2027 budget to make a King-sized signing. However, with a World Series window that may well slam shut next winter, maybe they embrace a heftier payroll than usual.

Los Angeles Angels : For two decades (2004-23), the Angels always ranked top nine in Opening Day payroll. But in Arte Moreno's final few years in charge, they've scaled back considerably on free agent spending. Maybe in year No. 1 with a new owner, they go grab King to pair with Reid Detmers and Walbert Ureña. It might at least make this team interesting for a change.

Los Angeles Dodgers : Here's your obligatory reminder that the Dodgers must always be considered a candidate to sign one of the better free agents available. But they do still have a Big Three of Yoshinobu Yamamoto, Blake Snell and Tyler Glasnow, possibly Shohei Ohtani returning to the mound and a deep stable of options for the Nos. 5 and 6 spots in the rotation, including Justin Wrobleski, Roki Sasaki and Emmet Sheehan. We'll see if that stops them, though.

St. Louis Cardinals : Only once in franchise history have the Cardinals signed a free agent to a contract with an AAV north of $17.5M, but that was the three-year, $75M deal with Sonny Gray just a couple winters ago. If they're willing to go back to that well, adding an ace to what was a 2026 rotation full of No. 3-4 starters could be a game-changer. And with virtually nothing presently on their 2027 payroll , they certainly have the room in the budget to do it.

Toronto Blue Jays : Of the six pitchers who made more than 10 starts for the Blue Jays in 2026, only Dylan Cease and Trey Yesavage are expected back in 2027. They do have José Soriano, though. Cody Ponce should be back after tearing his ACL in his season debut. Former top prospect Ricky Tiedemann might finally factor into the mix, too. Throw in Spencer Miles as an option and this rotation might be good/deep enough that they instead focus their offseason spending on a hitter like Randy Arozarena.

Michael King Landing Spot No. 5: Baltimore Orioles

Projected 2027 Starting Rotation Options : Shane Baz, Brandon Young, Kyle Bradish, Cade Povich, Trey Gibson

Notably, the Orioles have their own marquee arm hitting free agency in the form of Trevor Rogers. If they want to sign a guy who could start on Opening Day, they are quite familiar with one who already did so for them this season.

But they need to do something significant about this starting rotation, lest they sputter to yet another sub-.500 season with Pete Alonso and Gunnar Henderson on the roster.

Shane Baz is a fine pitcher, but he's not the ace of a World Series contender.

Likewise, Brandon Young had a respectable 2026 campaign, but he's not a Game 2-caliber starter in the postseason.

And who knows what Baltimore will get from Kyle Bradish in 2027 as he recovers from both a sports hernia and a tough season on the mound?

The good news is they've got some money to spend.

If, as expected, neither Zach Eflin's $25M mutual option nor Luis Robert Jr.'s $20M club option is exercised, both salaries will come off the books. Chris Bassitt's $18.5M salary will also no longer be part of the equation.

Even accounting for projected arbitration salaries, they're currently looking at a payroll at least $30M below their Opening Day payroll in each of the past two seasons—which is roughly what we expect Michael King's AAV to be.

Michael King Landing Spot No. 4: New York Mets

Projected 2027 Starting Rotation Options : Nolan McLean, Sean Manaea, Christian Scott, Zac Thornton, Tylor Megill, Jonah Tong, Jonathan Santucci

In recent years, the New York Mets have been none too shy about investing heavily in position players.

But since spending all that money on Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander only to go 75-87 in the one season they were together on the roster, they've shied away from shelling out the big bucks for starting pitchers. (The one exception was re-signing Sean Manaea to a three-year, $75M contract after his career-best run through 2024, and that decision hasn't aged well at all.)

Will they continue to operate that way and pay Juan Soto more than they pay their entire starting rotation in 2027? Or do they make a big move for a guy like Michael King to bolster this young rotation?

To some extent, Bo Bichette's $84M opt-out decision has to matter.

If he leaves, the Mets could roll with their top prospect, Jefferson Rojas, at the hot corner in 2027 and reallocate those "savings" to an ace-caliber free agent—maybe even Tarik Skubal.

If Bichette stays in Queens, though, he'll be one of their eight players with a combined luxury tax salary of more than $223M. And even with Steve Cohen's checkbook, they'd have to think about whether it's worth adding a pitcher with a roughly $30M AAV to the equation.

Michael King Landing Spot No. 3: Washington Nationals

Projected 2027 Starting Rotation Options : Cade Cavalli, Connelly Early, Andrew Alvarez, Josiah Gray, DJ Herz, Jake Irvin, Jackson Kent

Only once in franchise history have the Washington Nationals / Montreal Expos scored more runs than they did this year, doing so in 2019 en route to their only World Series title.

And now the front office owes it to those hitters to go out and do something about what has been one of the worst pitching staffs in the majors in the 2020s.

They certainly have the room in the budget to sign a guy like King, if not several Kings.

Cade Cavalli will be getting $4M in the first year of his recently signed extension. Keibert Ruiz will make $5M. CJ Abrams' salary will probably jump from $4.2M to a bit north of $10M in arbitration. But aside from the deferred money that they are somehow still paying both Stephen Strasburg and Max Scherzer, that's about it.

And we know the Lerners have money in the banana stand. Washington's year-end tax payroll was slightly north of $200M each year from 2017-19. They could/should be gearing up to take a page from the Detroit Tigers' playbook of recently reopening the checkbook in a big way after six to seven years of cutting back on spending amid a rebuild.

Maybe they don't go whole hog for Tarik Skubal, as they are literally still paying the price for the last time they gave an ace more than $200M. But put King atop this rotation alongside Cavalli—while maybe replacing the entire bullpen—and the Nats would be back in business for the first time since right before the pandemic.

Michael King Landing Spot No. 2: Chicago Cubs

Projected 2027 Starting Rotation Options : Justin Steele, Edward Cabrera, Ben Brown, Javier Assad, Colin Rea, Cade Horton (should return from Tommy John around the All-Star Break)

The Cubs played 19 games over the final three weeks of the regular season. The starting pitchers for those games were Shota Imanaga (four), Matthew Boyd (four), David Peterson (four), Clay Holmes (four) and Kevin Gausman (three).

Imanaga, Peterson and Gausman are unrestricted free agents, Boyd has a mutual option for 2027 that is unlikely to be exercised, and Holmes will almost certainly decline his $12M player option for next season.

Welcome to "Extreme Makeover: Cubs Rotation."

Given how much they are losing, though, their 2027 outlook...isn't actually that bad?

Steele's rehab from elbow surgery went miserably this year, but they hope he'll be back at full strength for Opening Day. They're certainly also hoping that Cabrera looks more like he did in 2025 with the Marlins than he did this season. And heading into next season, there will be much worse Nos. 4-5 tandems than Assad and Rea.

But there's no way they're going to just move on from an entire starting rotation without at least trying to make a big splash, right?

Boyd and Imanaga made a combined $37M in 2026. Fellow free agents Ian Happ and Seiya Suzuki combined for another $36M. And those are merely the big-ticket items for a team that has well north of $100M coming off the books this winter.

Curiously enough, Michael King has only made one appearance at Wrigley Field in his career, that coming in Game 3 of last year's wild card series, when he consecutively struck out Pete Crow-Armstrong, Dansby Swanson and Matt Shaw in his lone inning of work. But he could be a fixture within the friendly confines over the next few years.

Michael King Landing Spot No. 1: San Diego Padres

Projected 2027 Starting Rotation Options : Nick Pivetta, Randy Vásquez, Joe Musgrove?, Matt Waldron??, Yu Darvish???

As mentioned earlier, the Padres have a long list of free agents, including up to 11 pitchers .

Some good news is that Nick Pivetta's two-year, $32M player option was converted to a $14M club option because of how long he was on the IL this year. It's a near-certainty they'll bring him back, thanks to a lack of other comforting options.

Darvish missed all of 2026 ( and almost retired ) after a UCL internal brace surgery, but he might come back next year at 40 years old. Musgrove has missed the past two regular seasons after Tommy John surgery, but the Padres need him back on the mound in 2027. Waldron's knuckleball hasn't been fooling anyone in the majors with a 5.16 ERA thus far in his career.

And yet, those are three of the leaders in the clubhouse for spots in the 2027 rotation, even if Pivetta does stick around.

Long story short, there will definitely be a desire to re-up with King if and when he officially opts out of the two seasons left on his contract.

Considering he has a 2.88 ERA in 39 regular season starts at Petco Park over the past three years, one would assume he's at least open to the idea, too.

For what it's worth, this past winter, Cody Bellinger, Shota Imanaga and Ha-Seong Kim each either declined player options or exercised an opt-out clause before re-signing with the same team. Same goes for Nathan Eovaldi, Sean Manaea and Michael Wacha the previous offseason.

In other words, it's hardly unheard of, and the Padres feel like the early favorite to retain King's services.

articles.title: Ranking Yankees 2B Jazz Chisholm Jr.'s Top 5 Landing Spots in MLB Free Agency
articles.summary: When the New York Yankees were preparing for their 2026 season, Jazz Chisholm Jr. set some big goals for himself.
articles.body:
When the New York Yankees were preparing for their 2026 season, Jazz Chisholm Jr. set some big goals for himself.

He hoped to join Shohei Ohtani in MLB's 50-50 club. And then, he hoped to secure a free-agent contract worth $35 million per year over eight to 10 years.

So much for that. Chisholm had a disappointing year, going off for "only" 19 home runs and 41 stolen bases with a modest .711 OPS and 1.7 rWAR. The second baseman didn't have a particularly good postseason, with the Yankees' run ending in a three-game sweep at the hands of the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday.

As for Chisholm's prospects in free agency, Jon Heyman of the New York Post raised the question of whether the 28-year-old even deserves a $23.1 million qualifying offer from the Yankees. If that's the situation, his best play might be to make like Marcus Semien in 2021 and seek a one-year "prove it" deal for 2027.

With this in mind, let's identify five potential suitors for Chisholm and dive into why they make sense as landing spots for the two-time All-Star.

To be clear, the Reds are probably only going to be a match for Chisholm if he indeed decides to seek a one-year deal.

Any more than that, and their history in free agency suggests they'd sit this one out. They rank 26th out of 30 teams in free-agent spending since 1991, with a max of just $64 million for Nick Castellanos and Mike Moustakas.

On paper, though, this is about as clean as fits get. The Reds got an MLB-low -0.7 rWAR from the keystone this season, as well as a 90 wRC+ from the left side of the plate that tied for the second-worst mark in the league. Chisholm could help them address both issues with one signing.

Besides, this organization badly needs to throw its fanbase a bone after the year it just had. Pairing Chisholm with Elly De La Cruz and Sal Stewart and letting the three cook at Great American Ball Park for at least one year would do nicely.

Under Arte Moreno, the Angels have occasionally come out of the woodwork with a Brinks truck for a star free agent.

Well, now they have a new—and potentially much better—owner coming aboard. The sale of the franchise to Stan Kroenke still needs approval, but it is expected to become official sometime in the first quarter of 2027 .

That could give the Angels time to make a run at Chisholm if he's still available. He might not be if he sets his sights on a one-year deal early in the winter. But if he insists on holding out for a multi-year offer, L.A. could be a late-arriving hope.

What's for sure is that they need an influx of star talent after losing 100 games for the first time in their history this season. They specifically need it at a second base spot which produced only 0.4 rWAR, and having Chisholm and Zach Neto as a double play combination would surely help reinvigorate a jaded fanbase.

Sticking in Southern California, the Padres are a step ahead of the Angels as far as ownership changes go. Kwanza Jones and José E. Feliciano officially took control in August.

Though they've already been able to celebrate their first playoff run, they'll soon experience what seems like an annual rite of passage in San Diego: a roster in need of considerable refurbishing.

Starting pitching will need to be a priority, but another bat should also be a must. The Padres specifically need more left-handed thump after getting just a .385 SLG from that side of the plate. They could also use more offensive production at second base, where Jake Cronenworth struggled in 2026.

Also, does anyone else get the sense that San Diego would be a good spot for Chisholm's energy? He plays with a chip on his shoulder, and that's been the Padres' whole vibe as they have fought the Los Angeles Dodgers for control of the NL West throughout the 2020s.

Predicting the Outcome for Each Team's Top Free Agent 🔮

Ranking Michael King, Casey Mize's Top Landing Spots

The Tigers got two pretty solid seasons out of Gleyber Torres at second base, including an All-Star campaign in 2025. Like Chisholm, though, he's about to be a free agent.

For the Tigers, swapping out Torres for Chisholm at second base would be a play for greater upside. Torres is sneaky-good at getting on base, but with little in the way of power or speed. Chisholm was a 30-30 guy just last year. He's also a plus defender despite his occasional lapses in judgment .

Chisholm's speed is especially needed in Detroit after the Tigers stole only 58 bases this year. That's just 17 more than Chisholm had on his own, and it amounts to refusing to play a game that a team really should be playing in this day and age.

The Tigers could use Chisholm's energy, too. Even if they had bigger problems this year, his outgoing personality would bring a different dynamic to the roster. Signing Chisholm to be part of a double-play combo with Kevin McGonigle would be a step in the right direction.

Ernie Clement was the AL's leading vote-getter for the All-Star Game this year. Would the Blue Jays really bump him off second base for Chisholm?

Well, yeah. Or at least, they should. Clement can play everywhere, after all, and Toronto's offense needs upside that he simply can't provide. Somehow, the Blue Jays finished last in the league in scoring this season.

It's going to take a Vladimir Guerrero Jr. rebound and multiple new faces for the Blue Jays' offense to recover in 2027. To the latter end, Chisholm is one of the best free agents they'll be able to get this winter. After hitting just 152 homers (30th in MLB) and stealing 75 bases (27th in MLB), they badly need his power and speed.

Given the chip on his shoulder, it also wouldn't be the worst thing if Chisholm had 13 chances every year to take it to the Yankees. Even if we can agree he deserved to become a platoon player this year, he clearly didn't appreciate it .

Stats courtesy of Baseball Reference , FanGraphs and Baseball Savant .

articles.title: Aaron Judge Says Yankees Need to Go 'All-In' to Build Roster in Video After MLB Playoffs Exit
articles.summary: On the heels of being swept out of the playoffs by the Tampa Bay Rays, Aaron Judge knows how he would like to see the New York Yankees front office respond to get them back to being a World Series contender in 2027.
articles.body:
On the heels of being swept out of the playoffs by the Tampa Bay Rays, Aaron Judge knows how he would like to see the New York Yankees front office respond to get them back to being a World Series contender in 2027.

After the Yankees' 4-3 loss in Game 3 against the Rays on Wednesday, Judge said the organization needs to go "all-in" to upgrade the roster by "finding certain players or personnel, whatever we need, you got to go out there and get it."

Judge went on to say it's "tough to say" if the front office has done enough recently because the Yankees are competitive every season, but "that's not good enough" for how high the expectations always are for the franchise.

This season, for instance, New York was one of only three teams with a payroll over $300 million. The New York Mets ($346.7 million) and Los Angeles Dodgers ($339.3 million) are the others.

If the Yankees want to stay around the $300 million mark, they won't have a lot of room to operate as things currently stand. They have $276.4 million in payroll allocations on the books for 2027.

It's overly simplistic to say Judge being healthy might have swung the entire American League toward the Bronx, but the numbers show how much their offensive production suffered without him in 2026.

In the three months Judge missed from June 1 through Sept. 7 due to a stress fracture in his rib, the Yankees had a bottom-five offense in MLB.

The fact that New York's lineup was so reliant on one player, albeit arguably the best hitter of this generation, does lend credence to Judge's point about the front office needing to do a better job of adding talent.

There really isn't a lot the Yankees need to do to take the next step beyond the lineup. They had the best team ERA in MLB during the regular season and were an above-average defensive club by defensive runs saved.

One potential area of concern is the Yankees had the fifth-oldest roster in MLB this season. Judge will turn 35 in April. Gerrit Cole turned 36 on Sept. 8. Max Fried will be 33 on Jan. 18.

The Yankees have been a strong developmental organization, particularly on the pitching side with Cam Schlittler likely to win the AL Cy Young award. Ben Rice had a star-making season with 41 homers.

It is rare for Judge to speak out like this in public, so the fact he did after the Yankees were swept in the ALDS might suggest some frustration on his part or at least an attempt to put pressure on general manager Brian Cashman and his staff going into the offseason.

articles.title: Jazz Chisholm Jr. Talks Boos From Yankees Fans in Video After Playoff Exit, 'It's Just Confusing'
articles.summary: Second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. commented on the fans at Yankee Stadium booing him Wednesday night during the New York Yankees' season-ending, 4-3 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 3 of the American League Division Series.
articles.body:
Second baseman Jazz Chisholm Jr. commented on the fans at Yankee Stadium booing him Wednesday night during the New York Yankees' season-ending, 4-3 loss to the Tampa Bay Rays in Game 3 of the American League Division Series.

Asked by reporters if the fans' reaction was hurtful, Chisholm said, "It doesn't hurt. It's just confusing because it's the playoffs and we're trying to win games. So, you're booing a guy that's playing trying to help the team win, and you're hearing boos instead of trying to hype guys up."

Chisholm completed his point about not being "hurt" by the boos by pointing out that he has seen superstar slugger Aaron Judge get booed by the Yankee Stadium faithful before too.

Despite the Yankees facing a right-handed starting pitcher Wednesday night in Nick Martinez, the lefty-hitting Chisholm did not get the start.

That is likely due to the fact that the two-time All-Star failed to record a hit in six at-bats over the first two games of the ALDS. He also committed a crucial throwing error that allowed a run to score in Game 2.

However, Chisholm entered Game 3 as a pinch hitter in the seventh inning of Game 3 with manager Aaron Boone seemingly hoping that he could deposit one into the short porch in right field.

That didn't come to fruition, though, as Chisholm popped out in foul territory in his first at-bat, and then grounded into a fielder's choice in the ninth inning.

Chisholm did steal second base after that, but it didn't matter, as Trent Grisham struck out to end the game and the Yanks' season.

It is possible that the ninth-inning stolen base could prove to be Chisholm's final action as a Yankee, as he is set to become a free agent during the offseason.

Jazz showed what he could do at his best in 2025, posting 31 home runs and 31 stolen bases, but after seeing his homer total drop to 19 and his batting average dip to .231 this season, it is easy to envision the 28-year-old veteran playing elsewhere in 2027.

articles.title: Dua Lipa, Callum Turner Take Photo With MLB Superfan 'Marlins Man' During Yankees' ALDS G3 vs. Rays
articles.summary: Yankee Stadium on Wednesday featured a superstar meeting between MLB superfan Marlins Man, Dua Lipa and Callum Turner during the Tampa Bay Rays-New York Yankees playoff game.
articles.body:
Yankee Stadium on Wednesday featured a superstar meeting between MLB superfan Marlins Man, Dua Lipa and Callum Turner during the Tampa Bay Rays-New York Yankees playoff game.

Marlins Man, aka Laurence Leavy, posted a selfie from his seats behind home plate with the recently-married celebrity couple even though he "had no idea" who they were.

Marlins Man also said Dua Lipa was "super nice" and maybe the "best ever celebrity" he's met.

At one point, Marlins Man responded to someone on X by pointing out this was Dua Lipa's first-ever MLB game and first time eating a hot dog.

Turner and Dua Lipa got some help from Yankees fans about the customs of the game, including standing up and cheering when a hitter on the opposing team gets two strikes against them.

This has been a busy week for Dua Lipa, who made it to the Bronx on Wednesday night after visiting Paris two days earlier for the Chanel fashion show.

Turner spent part of his summer in the tri-state area working on the remake of Possession that filmed in New Jersey ahead of its planned release in August 2027.

Unfortunately for the Yankees, the presence of Turner and Dua Lipa was not enough to change their fortunes. Their season ended with a 4-3 loss to the Rays in Game 3 of the ALDS.

articles.title: Rays troll Yankees by blasting team's victory song in clubhouse during ALDS celebration
articles.summary: The Rays were extremely happy to vanquish a division rival.
articles.body:
After every victory at home, the New York Yankees blast the "Theme from New York, New York" in the clubhouse. It's become a tradition, one that's stood in place — with some alterations — since the 1980s. The Yankees have done a lot of winning since then.

Unfortunately for the team, traditions are a pretty easy target for tomfoolery when the Yankees lose. The team learned that the hard way Wednesday night, as the Tampa Bay Rays celebrated their American League Division Series sweep over the Yankees by trolling the team with its own victory song.

During the Rays' clubhouse celebration, the team blasted "Theme from New York, New York." Members of the team sang along and started swaying to the music.

Rays players clearly delighted in the fact that they were able to eliminate one of their biggest rivals in three straight games. But no player had more fun than Junior Caminero, who mimed sweeping Yankees fans out of the stadium following the contest.

Caminero also broke out multiple impressions of former Yankees radio announcer John Sterling's signature call after victories. After every Yankees victory, Sterling would announce, "The Yankees win. Theeeeeeeeeee Yankees win."

Caminero's version changed one key word. You can probably guess which one.

With the win in the series, the Rays advanced to the American League Championship Series for the third time in franchise history. The team has never lost in the round, advancing to the World Series in each of their previous visits.

The Rays don't know who they'll face in the ALCS just yet. After jumping out to a 2-0 lead in the series, the Chicago White Sox dropped Wednesday's game to the Cleveland Guardians. The White Sox can advance to the ALCS on Thursday with a win over Cleveland. If Chicago loses, both teams will play a winner-take-all Game 5 on Saturday.

articles.title: Rays Troll Yankees With 'New York, New York' in Celebration Video After MLB Playoff Series Win
articles.summary: Frank Sinatra's New York, New York blares over the sound system after every New York Yankees win at Yankee Stadium, but the Tampa Bay Rays made it their own celebratory tune on Wednesday night.
articles.body:
Frank Sinatra's New York, New York blares over the sound system after every New York Yankees win at Yankee Stadium, but the Tampa Bay Rays made it their own celebratory tune on Wednesday night.

Following a 4-3 win over the Yankees in Game 3 of the American League Division Series, the Rays celebrated in their locker room by playing and singing along to New York, New York :

Predicting the Outcome for Each Team's Top Free Agent 🔮

The win eliminated the Yanks from the playoffs and allowed the Rays to advance to the American League Championship Series for the third time in franchise history.

After taking the first two games of the series at home, the Rays traveled to New York in hopes of putting a bow on things.

That is exactly what they did on Wednesday, thanks largely to a two-run home run by Victor Mesa Jr. in the sixth inning to take a 4-2 lead.

The Rays also got the benefit of a huge call in the bottom of the sixth on a long drive to left field by Yankees infielder Anthony Volpe that was initially ruled a home run.

After review, it was determined that a fan reached too far over the wall to touch the ball, turning the hit from a game-tying, two-run shot to an RBI double.

The Yankees did not score again from that point forward, as relievers Griffin Jax, Cam Booser, Kevin Kelly and Bryan Baker shut the door the rest of the way for Tampa.

With the loss, New York fell short of the ALCS for the second straight year and third time in the past four seasons.

Meanwhile, the Rays will await the winner of the other ALDS between the Chicago White Sox and Cleveland Guardians, and they figure to be massive favorites to reach the World Series regardless of who their opponent is.

articles.title: Updated MLB Payroll Rankings for Dodgers, Rays Remaining Playoff Teams
articles.summary: With five teams still remaining in the MLB playoffs, the Los Angeles Dodgers' payroll is almost as high as the other four teams combined.
articles.body:
With five teams still remaining in the MLB playoffs, the Los Angeles Dodgers' payroll is almost as high as the other four teams combined.

One of the Dodgers, Milwaukee Brewers, Tampa Bay Rays, Chicago White Sox and Cleveland Guardians will end the 2026 season as the World Series champions.

Here are the payrolls for those five clubs, via Spotrac .

Wednesday saw three of the 10 highest-spending teams lose to end their seasons. The New York Yankees ($308,336,780), Atlanta Braves ($263,462,438) and San Diego Padres ($226,252,714) all went home.

Eight of the top-10 teams in payroll made the postseason, but the Dodgers are the only one from that group still playing. Most of those teams have beat up on each other so far.

For instance, the Yankees eliminated the Boston Red Sox; the Padres knocked out the Cubs; and the Braves beat the Philadelphia Phillies prior to being defeated by the Dodgers in the NLDS.

The only division series still going is between the two AL Central teams. The Guardians staved off elimination with a 9-3 win over the White Sox to force a Game 4 on Thursday.

As those two clubs duke it out, the Rays get to patiently wait for their opponent after sweeping the Yankees. They will be making their third appearance in the ALCS, having previously reached the World Series in 2008 and 2020.

Over in the senior circuit, the NLCS matchup most expected to happen came to fruition with the Dodgers and Brewers in a rematch from last year. They were the top two teams in MLB by record during the regular season, with the Brewers winning 103 games and Dodgers close behind with 100 victories.

Their 2025 series was a four-game sweep by the Dodgers in which their pitching held Milwaukee to a total of four runs.

If the Dodgers advance, they will be the first team to reach the World Series in three consecutive years since the Yankees did it in four straight seasons from 1998 to 2001.

Game 1 between the Dodgers and Brewers will be played on Sunday. The ALCS will begin on Monday with the Rays hosting the winner of the Guardians-White Sox series.

articles.title: MLB sends memo to owners, executives outlining how they should act, operate during upcoming lockout
articles.summary: MLB is preparing its employees in the case of a lockout.
articles.body:
The most exciting time in the baseball season is here, but MLB is already focused on the upcoming lockout. In preparation for the expiration of the collective-bargaining agreement (CBA), the league reportedly sent a 34-page memo to owners and executives on Oct. 1 detailing how those individuals should act and operate during the lockout, per The Athletic.

If a lockout is initiated, teams and players are prohibited from discussing business. This often means players and team executives are unable to converse while there's no new CBA in place.

That will once again be the case this time around, as the memo urged against teams sending holiday cards to players ... unless they send them before the lockout. Team executives are permitted to attend player weddings over the offseason, but cannot talk business with any players there.

If team executives happen to run into a player unexpectedly, those executives are allowed to "be cordial" in conversations with the player.

Additionally, the league's website will once again remove videos and player images during the lockout, per The Athletic. That includes altering articles and headlines.

"Player images (including from their profile pages) and videos would be removed, and player names and pictures would be removed from article headlines."

The league took the same tactic in 2021.

MLB also sent along talking points executives should use when asked about the lockout or the upcoming CBA negotiations. As far as the 2027 season is concerned, executives were told to communicate they expected the season to go off as planned. They were also told they can communicate that season-ticket holders will be credited or refunded if games are canceled.

While all of that sounds ominous, the league did say its ultimate goal was "to exhaust every realistic option to achieve our goal of reaching an agreement with the Players Association." That messaging might ring hollow in a document that largely focuses on what to do once a lockout is in place, however.

Any hope of a deal coming together before the expiration of the current CBA on Dec. 1 seems low. Much like the last time the CBA expired, both the league and its players are expected to engage in a lengthy, contentious negotiation that will likely span months after the current CBA expires.

Once the threat of canceled games becomes more real, both sides will feel more pressure to come to a deal so the 2027 season is not lost.

articles.title: Tampa Bay Rays, led by unsung heroes and offseason additions, defeat the Yankees amid chaos in the Bronx to punch a ticket to the ALCS
articles.summary: The Rays spent this past offseason shaking up their roster. Now they're headed to the ALCS for the third time in franchise history.
articles.body:
NEW YORK — Down 2-0 in the best-of-five ALDS to the Tampa Bay Rays, the New York Yankees were counting on their home crowd to provide the necessary boost to help them climb back into the series. In the sixth inning of Game 3 on Wednesday, the Bronx crowd tried to give their beloved ballclub a helping hand — literally. Unfortunately, that gesture fell beyond the regulated boundaries of home-field advantage.

Anthony Volpe — inserted into the starting lineup in place of Jazz Chisholm Jr. with manager Aaron Boone seeking a spark for his morose offense — strolled to the plate against Rays right-hander Griffin Jax with two outs and the Yankees down 4-2. Volpe represented the tying run, with rookie George Lombard Jr. on first after drawing a walk. When Jax fired a 96-mph sinker inside on a 1-0 count, Volpe lifted the ball with force, sending it soaring into the New York sky at a 42-degree launch angle. On contact, it looked like a harmless flyout to end the inning. But the ball stayed almost stuck in the air, willed by the eager crowd to float toward the seats.

Rays left fielder Victor Mesa Jr. drifted back, tracking the ball's descent. But as he leapt to try to snag the ball, a pair of Yankees fans just above the fence reached over and interrupted his attempt. The ball clanged off their hands and hopped the fence for what initially appeared to be the game-tying, two-run blast the home crowd was hoping for — until replay review revealed a less-flattering reality.

Home plate umpire and crew chief Dan Bellino announced to the sellout crowd of 48,865 what was blatantly obvious to anyone watching at home, with the benefit of multiple camera angles: It was spectator interference, and the ball would not have cleared the wall without assistance.

It was ruled a double rather than an out, with the replay center determining that Mesa would not have caught the ball, but Lombard would have scored from first. Volpe, having rounded the bases and returned to a tunnel of high-fives in the rejuvenated Yankees dugout, sheepishly sauntered back to second base. Jax then struck out Spencer Jones on three pitches to end the inning.

A tie game it was not. The Yankees had cut the Rays' lead to one, but had more work to do if they wanted to extend their season another day.

Another run never arrived. The 4-4 score that lingered for a few minutes on the giant Yankee Stadium video board never came to fruition. The corrected tally, 4-3, stayed intact for the final three frames of the ballgame. As a result, the Rays completed their sweep of the Yankees in fitting fashion : with contributions from a potpourri of unheralded players who are thriving with Tampa Bay after flying under the radar elsewhere.

Coming off the franchise's worst campaign in nearly a decade — 77 wins and a fourth-place finish in the AL East — the Rays spent this past offseason shaking up their roster. The bulk of the headlines Tampa Bay made with its transactional activity involved notable subtractions, rather than additions. Longtime closer Pete Fairbanks departed in free agency. Brandon Lowe, the team's longest tenured player, was traded to Pittsburgh. Rotation mainstay Shane Baz was dealt to Baltimore. Outfield staple Josh Lowe was shipped to Anaheim. It was clear the Rays were going to look different in 2026.

The moves made to upgrade the roster throughout the winter, meanwhile, attracted far less attention. But fast-forward to the Rays' rowdy celebration on Wednesday in the visitors' clubhouse at Yankee Stadium, and it's clear they would not be popping bottles without a series of those stealthy moves executed last winter.

Seemingly shirtless before all of his teammates in the postgame champagne celebration was right-hander Nick Martinez, who signed a one-year, $13 million free-agent deal back in February and started Game 3 on the mound for Tampa Bay. His effort Wednesday — two runs allowed over 3 ⅔ innings before making way for a quintet of stellar relief outings — was modest relative to his spectacular regular-season contributions.

But it was no accident that the Rays felt confident giving him the ball for his first career postseason start at age 36; he spent the past eight months earning the admiration of the entire clubhouse. Not only did he enjoy a bona fide breakout on the mound en route to his first All-Star appearance, but Martinez also immediately assumed a leadership role as an affable connector of all corners of the clubhouse.

"He's the guy that's organizing team events," said catcher Liam Hicks, who joined the Rays at the August trade deadline and instantly recognized Martinez's outsized role away from the ballpark. "He's just the man. He's the guy that you can go to for anything."

"Nick is everybody's biggest cheerleader the days he doesn't pitch and maybe more so on the days he does pitch," manager Kevin Cash said. "He puts a smile on everybody's face because he cares so much. He's always asking, 'what can I do? How can I help you?' He's been instrumental to our success."

"He brought this team together like nobody could," Rays hitting coach Ozzie Timmons said. "That's why they call him the Prez — he comes here, he brings that energy every day, no matter how things are going. He's always positive."

That Martinez has emerged as not just a key clubhouse presence but also a crucial member of the pitching staff for the best team in the American League is the latest chapter in a truly unique baseball journey. A Miami native, Martinez was primarily a shortstop at Fordham University before converting full-time to the mound upon entering pro ball with the Rangers. He spent four years in the majors with Texas before heading across the globe to pitch in Japan, where he found another gear with a reinvented arsenal and improved command. After returning to the big leagues in 2022, Martinez excelled in a swingman role with San Diego and Cincinnati before joining Tampa Bay as a full-time rotation member.

Last year, when Martinez was with Cincinnati, the Reds called up an outfielder named Ryan Vilade in June, after claiming him off waivers from St. Louis a couple of weeks earlier. Martinez recognized his name but struggled to place him immediately.

"We picked him up, and I'm like, 'Man, I know that last name,'" Martinez recalled. "I remember his dad."

James Vilade was a coach for the Frisco RoughRiders, the Rangers' Double-A affiliate that Martinez pitched for in 2013 and 2014.

"I hadn't seen him in 12 years. He comes up like, 'Hey, I'm Vilade — I was your bat boy [with Frisco].' I was like, 'Oh s***, what's up, dude?! Good to see you again!'"

The reunion in Cincinnati was brief. Vilade appeared in one game with the Reds as a defensive substitution — in a Martinez start, as it were — before returning to Triple-A. But just a few months later, he became the first player to change teams during the offseason. On Nov. 3, the day the Dodgers held their World Series parade, the Rays acquired Vilade from Cincinnati in exchange for cash considerations.

"I was shocked," Vilade said of the trade while soaked in champagne and surrounded by cigar smoke. A couple hours earlier, he had provided the first big swing of the ballgame, a go-ahead solo homer to the short porch in right field off Yankees ace lefty Max Fried that made it 2-1 Tampa Bay. "It kind of blindsided me. But man, I'm so happy they did."

Vilade was a top prep prospect and second-round pick by the Rockies out of high school in 2017. He never stuck in Colorado and bounced around a few other organizations without getting a prolonged run in the majors. But he was terrific in Triple-A for St. Louis and Cincinnati in 2025, making him an intriguing platoon target for Tampa Bay.

"When Erik [Neander] called me in November and said, 'Hey, listen, this is going to be your job. You're going to handle left-handed pitching,'" he recalled, "I felt from that time that this is my role. I felt pretty good."

On cue, the Rays' president of baseball operations appeared, similarly drenched and rocking pink goggles for eye protection.

"A+," Neander proclaimed, beaming as he gave Vilade a big hug. "He deserves this."

"We should have done it sooner," Neander said as he bounced away. "We screwed up. We should've gotten him last year."

Like Martinez, Vilade brings a dose of positive hype and uplifting spirit to the clubhouse, even beyond what he does on the field.

"He brings the energy every single night," said Rays starter Drew Rasmussen, whose no-hit bid in Game 1 set the tone for Tampa Bay's sweep . "But then on top of it, what he's done against left-handed pitching all year has been unbelievable. We couldn't have asked for anything more."

With just 71 major-league plate appearances to his name entering this season, Vilade hit .272/.341/.477 with seven homers in 170 plate appearances against left-handers. And that was before his stadium-silencing moon shot off Fried.

"Just watch this place," Rasmussen said, motioning to Martinez and Vilade in the center of the clubhouse dance party. "It revolves around those two."

Vilade's swing against Fried was pivotal, but it would not have been enough on its own. The Yankees drew even shortly after on a Spencer Jones RBI double.

So in the top of the sixth, it was yet another offseason addition's turn to make an impact in the series clincher. A few days before they signed Martinez in February, the Rays acquired Victor Mesa Jr. from Miami in a trade for minor-league infielder Angel Brachi. The son of a legendary Cuban player and manager, Mesa harbored some prospect value coming up with the Marlins and debuted with them in 2025 but didn't seem to fit into their long-term plans.

He looked like depth for the Rays at the time of the deal and began this season in Triple-A. But after being recalled in late May, Mesa established himself as an every-day outfielder for Tampa Bay, thanks in large part to his ability to hit against pitchers from both sides. That comfort was on display in Game 3, as the lefty-swinging Mesa swatted a first-pitch sweeper from the southpaw Fried for a two-run homer that made it 4-2 Rays in the sixth — notching the fourth run that would ensure victory by the end of the night.

"Awesome human being," Rasmussen said of Mesa. "He's going to be a superstar."

Awaiting Mesa at home plate: face of the franchise Junior Caminero, who also joined the Rays in an offseason trade that seemed insignificant at the time.

This is what the Rays do. No transaction can be dismissed. Lacking the financial might of many of their biggest rivals, winning on the margins is paramount for Tampa Bay. And Neander and his front office have proven time and again that they can construct rosters capable of keeping pace with — or, in this case, downright dominating — the higher-salaried competition.

"This is the first playoff series I've ever won," a glowing Rasmussen said. "We were one-and-done in 2020 because I was with Milwaukee. One-and-done in '21. One-and-done in '22. One-and-done in '23. So to see one go through the uprights is really nice."

"It's unbelievable to do it with this group," he added. "I bet you you can walk around this room. No one needs credit. Everyone's willing to do the job that's asked of them, and it just makes it such a fun environment to be in."

From one of the best pitchers in the American League in Rasmussen to an unsung platoon bat in Vilade, the 2026 Rays are flying high. Next up: the ALCS, for just the third time in franchise history.

"We're pretty happy to be here right now," Rasmussen said. "But the job's not finished."

"I'm grateful that I landed here," Vilade added. "I love this team. I love this organization.

With the Brewers leading 3-1 in the bottom of the eighth inning, Padres third baseman Manny Machado hit a ball deep to right-centerfield, but Mitchell tracked it down and elevated ever so slightly to prevent a home run:

Predicting the Outcome for Each Team's Top Free Agent 🔮

Had the ball left the yard, it would have tied the game at 3-3 and given the Padres new life in the game and the series.

Mitchell was the unquestioned star of the game for the Brewers in all facets, as he thrived at the plate in addition to his defense.

After posting the best record in Major League Baseball during the regular season at 103-59, the Brewers are now back in the NLCS for a second consecutive year.

Awaiting them is a rematch with the Los Angeles Dodgers, who have won back-to-back World Series and are trying for the first three-peat since the New York Yankees from 1998 to 2000.

articles.title: Reviewing World Series 2026 Picks from MLB Experts for Final Series on the Bracket
articles.summary: The 2026 MLB playoff field was nearly sliced in half Wednesday night.
articles.body:
The 2026 MLB playoff field was nearly sliced in half Wednesday night.

Amid the carnage of wipe-out Wednesday, the Atlanta Braves, New York Yankees and San Diego Padres were all sent packing. The Cleveland Guardians, meanwhile, were the only team trapped in a deficit to live to see another day.

The coronation of the next World Series champion forever creeps closer, but maybe it's not moving along fast enough. Impatient fans, at least, might want to know that champion's identity sooner than later, so we'll look to the latest expert predictions and oddsmakers' lines to peak into their crystal-ball readings.

Five MLB franchises remain without a World Series title. A few experts from ESPN think the Milwaukee Brewers might be removing themselves from that unfortunate bunch.

In a recent batch of bold playoff predictions , three of ESPN's experts formed their prognostications around the Brewers winning big.

Tristan Cockcroft called for Milwaukee's breakout star Jackson Chourio to "become the 10th player to win LCS and World Series MVPs." Eric Karabell predicted a combined no-hitter for Jacob Misiorowski, Abner Uribe and Trevor Megill in Game 1 of the World Series. AJ Mass, meanwhile, had predicted the Brewers to "trail in every playoff game en route to a championship," though Milwaukee already torpedoed that one, as it never trailed in Wednesday's win.

That's a good amount of support for a squad that has never tasted championship glory before, but it's hard to say that it's undeserved. The Brewers, who won an MLB-best (and franchise-record) 103 games this season, have this postseason's highest OPS (.688) and second-lowest ERA (1.80).

Two-Time Defending Champs Aren't the Favorites?

Ahead of this postseason, The Athletic had "more than 20" of its MLB experts make World Series predictions. That group did not make the Los Angeles Dodgers—winners of the past two World Series—the most popular pick.

The Brewers ran away with the poll and garnered 56 percent of the vote. The Tampa Bay Rays took second with 24 percent, while the Dodgers received just 16 percent of the vote. The Brewers and Rays are both viable picks, but that's still less support than you'd expect for a club with this much star power and this level of recent dominance.

"No team carries as much October hype as Los Angeles," Katie Woo wrote. "There are rightful concerns over the drop-off in production from Shohei Ohtani and Freddie Freeman, but their rotation of aces should carry them through any qualms on the offense. It's the Dodgers' title to lose, and they know it."

Oddsmakers agree with that assessment, but if the majority of Woo's colleagues are right, this year's title won't make it back to L.A.

articles.title: Now Is the Time For the New York Yankees to Burn It Down
articles.summary: It's been 17 years. A decade plus seven of the New York Yankees walking right up to the line of being a championship-caliber team and stopping right there.
articles.body:
It's been 17 years. A decade plus seven of the New York Yankees walking right up to the line of being a championship-caliber team and stopping right there.

If it's an elaborate Andy Kaufman-esque prank by Hal Steinbrenner, Brian Cashman and Aaron Boone, the commitment to the bit is almost impressive. Yet Yankees fans aren't laughing. Far from it, in fact.

The Yankee Stadium crowd's reaction says it all after the Yankees were swept out of the 2026 playoffs by the Tampa Bay Rays on Wednesday. When Trent Grisham struck out with the tying run in scoring position, there wasn't one of those collective groans, followed by pained silence. There were loud, unmistakable boos.

A fanbase doesn't revert to boos in that situation if the outcome is genuinely shocking. Or, at the very least, if the ride there was fun.

Boos like that happen only when the jig is up, especially when that exact moment of defeat has become an annual rite of passage. The Yankees keep selling their fans false hope, and they're clearly tired of buying in only to get conned. Those boos say, "Not this crap again."

They want 27 World Series titles to become 28. Maybe, just maybe , it's time for the organization to get the message.

What Brian Cashman and Aaron Boone Have Done to the Yankees

Huh? What's that? The Yankees have had 34 consecutive winning seasons? Cashman has been in the front office for all of them? Boone has been in the manager's chair for the last nine?

It's the championships, stupid, and any attempt to label Yankees fans as spoiled for such high expectations misses the mark. They're not blind to the team's history , nor are they blind to the fact that the Yankees remain a business behemoth. Per Forbes , it's an $8.5 billion franchise that raked in $710 million in revenue last year.

There's no excuse for this team not to be at the top of the baseball world with some consistency. The fact that they have done so just once in 25 years inevitably makes one look around and ask, "Who the hell is running this place, anyway?"

Defenders of Cashman and Boone are out there. Boone 's own players consistently praise him , with three-time MVP Aaron Judge generally serving as his strongest ally. At any time, a veritable army of reporters goes to bat for Cashman for all he's accomplished .

True, Boone is good with the media and an effective heat shield for his players. And true, Cashman probably doesn't get enough credit for his development wins . He's the guy who believed in Judge and Cam Schlittler, and who can pat himself on the back for Ben Rice, George Lombard Jr. and Spencer Jones.

Yet if they get to own the positives of the modern-day Yankees experience, they must also own the negatives.

For all the Yankees' excellence at hitting home runs ( Fact Check: True ) and blowing away opposing hitters ( Fact Check: True ), what has mattered more in recent Octobers is just how bad they are at playing the actual game of baseball. Their collective proneness to mental gaffes and physical comedy is what doomed them in the 2024 World Series. This year, they did the same in Game 2 of the ALDS .

Cashman and Boone's ongoing failure to fix the problem* is only becoming a more glaring failure. Whereas the Yankees' fondness for homers in whiffs feels coded to the late-2010s, the 2020s are different. The Rays and Milwaukee Brewers prove that a team doesn't need the Los Angeles Dodgers' resources to play an "all of the above" style of baseball that is as overwhelming as it is aesthetically pleasing.

* So much for that weird " audit " in 2023, am I right?

The stacked failures are compounded by what was wasted. Those include the prime years of Judge, who might be the greatest right-handed hitter ever. They also include Gerrit Cole's prime years, a Cy Young Award winner who'll end his career with a compelling Hall of Fame case.

At some point, shouldn't somebody have to pay for this?

What Hal Steinbrenner Has Done to the Yankees

The answer is yes. A hard yes. Steinbrenner should absolutely fire Cashman and Boone and look elsewhere for people who can turn fresh perspectives into a better path forward for the Yankees.

Easier said than done, to be sure, and the Yankees only need to look across town at the Mets to see that. They also have vast wealth, and they arguably have an even greater desire to win. Yet Steve Cohen has yet to crack the code, at least in part because David Stearns isn't all he was cracked up to be .

But then there are the Dodgers. Setting aside the very real questions about Mark Walter's business empire, they have long since usurped the Yankees as the model for what happens when great power meets great ingenuity. Andrew Friedman is astoundingly good at running the front office, while Dave Roberts is everything a modern manager should be. They are the anti-Cashman and anti-Boone.

The dream for the Yankees is getting their own pair. An executive as good as Friedman at maintaing a talent pipeline even without the benefit of high draft picks and large international bonus pools. A manager as good as Roberts at both communicating and working the Xs and Os. And between the two of them, a shared philosophy on playing holistic ball. Homers and strikeouts are nice. Homers and strikeouts plus good defense and baserunning is better.

Will Steinbrenner actually move on from Cashman or Boone? Eh, don't count on it.

Boone has another year on his contract. Cashman does not, but is expected to sign a new deal. With a lockout looming, any effort by Steinbrenner to burn it all down and start anew faces a major complication.

What Steinbrenner can do either way this offseason is engage in some soul-searching. Or, if he wants to listen to Judge, he can merely look around for his wallet:

Steinbrenner probably doesn't want to hear it, given how often he's complained about having to operate with such high payrolls. Yet every time he does, he insults his fanbase's intelligence.

Again, these are the literal Yankees we're talking about. Back in 2011, the Yankees' year-end $216 million payroll accounted for 49 percent of $439 million in revenue. Last year, they had a $301.5 million payroll against $710 million in revenue. That's 42 percent.

If Steinbrenner isn't going to can Cashman or Boone, the best possible version of the coming offseason is one where he finally channels his late father, leaves no stone unturned, and doesn't leave any check unsigned. Tarik Skubal? Randy Arozarena? Teruaki Soto? Screw it, let 'em all come down.

Even that would feel like a half measure, though. Even with esteemed new guests, it'll be the same party if Cashman and Boone are still hosting. When asked to attend, fans would have every right to spin one of Yogi Berra's greatest quotes.

Nobody goes there anymore. It's too depressing.

articles.title: MLB Proposes 154-Game Regular Season, New Playoff Bracket Format amid CBA Talks with MLBPA
articles.summary: As the MLB playoffs continue, the league has announced new elements of its proposal amid the ongoing collective bargaining talks with the MLB Players Association.
articles.body:
As the MLB playoffs continue, the league has announced new elements of its proposal amid the ongoing collective bargaining talks with the MLB Players Association.

MLB's latest proposal includes implementing a 154-game regular season and expanding the Division Series round of the playoffs to a best-of-seven format.

Those changes, if approved, would go into effect in 2029. Another part of the proposal starting with the 2027 season would be to allow the higher-seeded clubs in the Wild Card and Division Series rounds to pick their opponents.

The MLBPA said in a statement on Thursday that it "will weigh in on these proposals and we will respond at the bargaining table." Of note, the players' union said the new proposal remains "contingent on players' agreement to a salary cap."

MLB has taken the unusual step of publicizing its various proposals to the union as the two sides continue to talk about a new CBA with the current one set to expire on Dec. 1.

Previous proposals made by the league include setting a weekly 26-man roster, with exceptions for things like injuries and transactions; and limiting the free-agency period to start on the Monday during the winter meetings through Dec. 21 to encourage more activity.

In June, MLB proposed an increase in the minimum salary, eliminating the qualifying offer system and reducing service time required to hit free agency from six years to five years.

Of course, the biggest potential hurdle facing the negotiations is a salary cap. The league has presented a cap proposal that would also include a salary floor and a 50-50 revenue split between the owners and players.

Players largely seem to be against any sort of cap system.

This latest proposal would have significant financial ramifications for MLB and the MLBPA. Even though it involves fewer regular-season games for all 30 teams, more playoff games would seemingly offset those losses.

Since the wild-card era began in 1995, the division series has always been a best-of-five. The 162-game regular season has been in place leaguewide since 1962.

The AL went to a 162-game season in 1961 after expanding from eight to 10 teams. The NL followed the next year after the New York Mets and Houston Colt .45s joined.

articles.title: MLB proposes returning to 154-game regular season, adopting best-of-seven division series and opponent selection in playoffs
articles.summary: The proposed changes are part of the league's desired salary cap and floor system.
articles.body:
Major League Baseball is proposing significant changes to the structure of both its regular season and postseason, as part of the league's desired salary cap and floor system, including permitting higher-seeded teams in the wild-card and division series to select their opponents.

MLB has suggested that, starting in 2029, the league return to a 154-game regular season for the first time since the 1960s. Back in 1961, the American League moved from 154 games to 162. The next year, the National League followed suit.

Also in 2029, MLB could begin putting on best-of-seven division series, the league explained online following a bargaining session with the MLB Players Association on Thursday.

Currently, division series take on a best-of-five format, whereas the American League and National League championship series are best-of-seven, as is the World Series. Stretching the ALDS and NLDS in that manner would allow for as many as eight more postseason games.

Plus, according to MLB, more prime-time matchups would be possible in that scenario, given that there'd be an increase in playoff off days, which simultaneously would provide pitchers extra rest.

As for the opponent selection wrinkle, MLB is recommending to enact that in 2027. Upon the conclusion of the regular season, the No. 3 seed, or third-best division winner in the AL and NL, would pick whether to play the No. 5 seed or No. 6 seed in their wild-card series.

Then, following the completion of the wild-card series, the No. 1 seed in the AL and NL would select which wild-card winner to face.

MLB spokesman Glen Caplin explained the reasoning behind the proposed changes in a statement on Thursday, via USA Today's Bob Nightengale :

"Returning to a 154-game schedule would allow us to introduce a weekly off day, which is good for player health, while also creating a new national broadcast window to showcase our most exciting teams and players. "A shorter regular season unlocks making October even better for our fans — with fewer weekday afternoon games, a longer Division Series and more opportunities to see the game's best pitchers on the biggest stage. "And allowing the top seeds to select their opponents in the first two rounds would create compelling storylines, intensify existing rivalries and create new ones."

Considering that a work stoppage could be imminent, MLB sent a 34-page memo to owners and executives on Oct. 1 , instructing them how they should operate during the lockout, as detailed in a Wednesday report from The Athletic's Evan Drellich .

articles.body: Over the hump and safely on the other side! We've got football tonight. We've got more playoff baseball. We've got a Yankees-less October to look forward to now! What a time to be alive. If we could only get the Dodgers outta here, it would be perfect. Give me White Sox-Brewers for all the marbles, just like God intended! On that note, welcome to a Thursday Nightcaps — the one where Lindsey Vonn works up a sweat as she gears up for a big birthday bash. LINDSEY VONN TURNS HEADS BY HER POOL, GISELE SNUBS TOM BRADY & THE RIDICULOUS FAKE OUTRAGE OVER US OPEN FANS Happy early 42nd birthday, Lindsey! What else? And by the way, for those too young to remember ... last night was a makeup call from the Baseball Gods 30 years (!!!) in the making: Yeah, I don't want to hear it, Yankees fans. articles.title: MLB proposes reverting schedule back to its old ways, but not without a wild postseason twist
articles.summary: Major League Baseball's proposal includes a 154-game season with weekly off-days and a best-of-seven Division Series starting as early as 2029.
articles.body: With a second lockout this decade pending, Major League Baseball owners are coming up with creative ways to get on the baseball field as planned in 2027. The league announced the proposal of a 154-game season, which would knock out eight games of the 162-game slate that was implemented in 1961. Owners also proposed the Division Series, which has been a best-of-five since its introduction in 1995, to be a best-of-seven, but with a wild twist. CLICK HERE FOR MORE OUTKICK SPORTS COVERAGE The highest seed in both the Wild Card and Division Series, owners proposed, would be given the ability to choose their opponents. "Returning to a 154-game schedule would allow us to introduce a weekly off-day, which is good for player health, while also creating a new national broadcast window to showcase our most exciting teams and players," MLB spokesman Glen Caplin said. "A shorter regular season unlocks making October even better for our fans -- with fewer weekday afternoon games, a longer Division Series and more opportunities to see the game’s best pitchers on the biggest stage. And allowing the top seeds to select their opponents in the first two rounds would create compelling storylines, intensify existing rivalries and create new ones." The opponent-choosing could perhaps be a reaction to this year's postseason format, in which the American League teams with the second- and third-best records, the New York Yankees and Boston Red Sox, will not see the Championship Series. YANKEES LEGENDS DEREK JETER, ALEX RODRIGUEZ DELIVER BLUNT POST-MORTEM ON TEAM: 'SOMETHING HAS TO CHANGE' Under the current format, rather than reseeding , the top seed in each league is automatically slated to face the winner of the 4-5 seed matchup, and the No. 2 seed goes against the 3-6 seed winner. The top three seeds are given to the three division winners (with the top two getting a bye), in record order, while the 4-6 seeds are given to the best non-division winners, also in record order. Thus, despite the second-best record in the AL, the Yankees were the fourth seed. With the 154-game schedule, which wouldn't be implemented until 2029, all teams would be off on Mondays , except for a rare nationally televised game or a holiday, in which case they would then be off that Thursday. Minor League Baseball is off every Monday, which has apparently been well received , as it's normally paired with a Sunday day game. Each team would also have a scheduled split doubleheader against each of its division rivals during the season. MLB teams originally played 154 games until the 1960s. articles.title: MLB proposes reduced schedule, new playoff format
articles.summary: Will Rob Manfred get his way with more changes to the sport?
articles.body:
Major League Baseball is heading straight for a work stoppage. Of that we are all almost 100% certain, as the latest Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA) expires on December 1st and both MLB and the MLB Players Association seem far apart on their biggest demands.

Chief among those is the scuttlebutt surrounding a potential cap and floor on total payrolls, something championed by several owners who see spending money as the lone way to compete in this sport (while the low-budget Tampa Bay Rays, Milwaukee Brewers, Chicago White Sox, and Cleveland Guardians all remain alive in the postseason).

A new wrinkle was leaked on Thursday however. As ESPN's Jeff Passan relayed , MLB proposed limiting the regular season to just 154 games (down from 162) as part of a structural overhaul of the regular and postseasons, with a caveat that Division Series would move to a best of seven format.

The other fun wrinkle here is that teams could then choose their opponents in the postseason, something that's been a topic of discussion just about every postseason as some Wild Card teams finish with records far greater than teams who won weak divisions (and therefore ended up with tougher overall paths to advancing).

Shaving off games during the regular season means shaving off money from gameday receipts, television contracts, and the like. It would also mean fewer overall game checks for players, so this would be something the MLBPA would likely be in opposition to unless there were significantly greater incentives for playing in the postseason. Such is life in a labor/owner negotiation, as there are billions of dollars riding on these seemingly small decisions.

I can only assume we'll get more interesting ideas leaked in this entire process. Keep in mind this is the same league with the same commissioner who gave us the Manfred Man, killed the shift, added pitch clocks and ABS, and slapped sponsor logos on helmets. Change does not seem to phase Rob Manfred, so change will 100% be on the table early and often within these negotiations all winter.
